newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn says new law possible if takeover code fails.
newsitem.headline: Bonn says new law possible if takeover code fails.

text.p: Germany may have to change its laws to force companies to abide by a takeover code if companies continue to lag in voluntarily accepting the constraints of the takeover rules, a finance ministry official said on Tuesday.

Joachim Henke, a departmental director at the finance ministry in Bonn, told a news conference, "We very much regret that the code has not gained a better response and that six companies in the (30-share) DAX index have still not agreed.

"If the acceptance remains so patchy for too long, then we would have to ask ourselves more and more whether we will have to make a law here as well, as we have done in other areas when another method did not work," he said.

For years Germany insisted that its gentlemen's agreement on another issue, insider trading, was fully adequate. But it moved in late 1993 to introduce laws against insider trading which threatened offenders with fines and imprisonment in a bid to improve the image of its financial centre.

Germany's image suffers in a similar way on takeover rules, as foreign companies say the lack of a specific merger code and a dense network of cross-shareholdings makes the German market difficult for outsiders to penetrate.

The German bourse introduced the voluntary takeover code in October 1995, calling on firms to pledge to stand by its rules, but the code has so far found the support of only 270 of a total of 683 listed companies. Just 61 of the DAX-100 companies have pledged to abide by the bourse's rules.

Under the terms of the gentlemen's agreement, a company that owns a stake of more than 50 percent in a target company is required to make an offer to outstanding shareholders, except in instances where an exemption has been granted.
The company has 18 months to make an offer, although the rules indicate that the price should be near to market levels at the time the offer is made.
Exemptions could be made when the company is an approved majority shareholder and is accepted as such by the target company's annual shareholder meeting.

The code in many ways resembles Britain's well-established takeover and mergers agreement, which is also not legally binding. But the British version calls for an offer at an earlier level, once a stake reaches 30 percent.
Deutsche Boerse AG on Monday launched an aggressive campaign for the takeover code, warning that firms that rejected it could be refused inclusion in German stock indices.
Inclusion in the major bourse indices -- the DAX-30, DAX-100 and 70-share M-DAX -- generally boosts turnover and liquidity in a stock, making it more attractive to investors.
Henke said that he hoped this would lead to a greater level of acceptance among companies.

The voluntary takeover code is intended to create greater transparency in the German market, which is so riddled with cross-shareholdings and merger defences that it has been nicknamed "Fortress Germany" by foreign predators.
This tightly-meshed network of industrial holdings means most takeovers here are friendly, family affairs.
Earlier this year, when Fried Krupp AG Hoesch Krupp made an apparently hostile bid for Thyssen AG , the attack ended in a friendly agreement to merge their two steel companies.

And in one of the most spectacular cases of an external hostile bid in recent years, Italian tyremaker Pirelli AG finally had to abandon its bid to acquire Continental AG after running into takeover barriers and the closed ranks of banks and industry.
But Henke warned that the lack of a takeover code would damage the standing of Germany in the long run.
"It is certainly not in the interests of Germany as a financial centre," he said.
